🚀 Hi! We are The Martians! 🪐

We are young space enthusiasts who love rockets, planets, astronauts, science, and technology!

For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are creating a fun Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer where kids can experience space missions, explore Mars, manage resources, and think like real astronauts.

We believe learning should be fun, creative, and adventurous!

Join our team, share your ideas, and let's explore the universe together! 🌎🚀

Dream Big. Explore Beyond!
summary: Mars Base Mission Trainer is an interactive Scratch game for ages 7-12. Players run a 5-Sol Mars outpost with five astronaut roles and five resources: Oxygen, Water, Food, Power and Safety. Each Sol they choose one action, and every action helps one system but costs another. A dust storm cuts solar power on Sol 3 and teaches kids to plan ahead. The game shows each action's cost on screen, so kids learn that space survival is about careful choices, not magic technology.
details:
Project Title: Mars Base Mission Trainer

Project Overview

Mars Outpost - The 5-Sol Survival Mission is an interactive educational game built using Scratch 3.0. It allows students to experience the challenges of managing a human outpost on Mars. Players take responsibility for a crew of five astronauts and must carefully manage essential resources such as water, oxygen, food, power, and safety.

The main goal is to survive five Martian days, called Sols, and successfully return the crew to Earth. The game teaches players that space exploration requires careful planning because every decision has benefits as well as costs.

The Problem

Space education often focuses on posters, facts, and information about planets. However, students do not always get opportunities to experience the real decisions astronauts may face during a space mission.

A Mars outpost would need limited resources, including water, oxygen, food, and electricity. It would also need protection from environmental challenges such as dust storms. Managing these resources is difficult because improving one resource may require using another.

Our project makes these challenges easier to understand through an interactive game.

Our Solution and How the Game Works

We developed a browser-playable Scratch 3.0 game in which players manage a Mars outpost. The mission follows a complete journey:

  1. Mission Briefing: Players learn about the mission and its objectives.
  2. Packing Supplies: Players select five essential supplies at the Earth depot.
  3. Launch: The rocket launches from Earth.
  4. Space Transit: The crew travels through space towards Mars.
  5. Mars Landing: The astronauts reach the Martian surface.
  6. Five-Sol Survival: Players manage resources and make one important decision during each Sol.
  7. Return to Earth: After surviving five Sols, the crew returns home.

The game has five crew roles: Water, Oxygen, Solar, Food, and Safety. Each role represents an important part of keeping the Mars outpost functioning.

At the beginning of every Sol, the outpost consumes resources:

  • Oxygen: 10 units
  • Water: 8 units
  • Food: 8 units
  • Power: 6 units
  • Safety: 5 units

Players can choose only ONE action per Sol and then press the End Sol button.

Available Actions and Resource Trade-offs

The resource changes are displayed on the screen before players choose an action. Green labels show resource gains, while red labels show resource costs.

Power is the most important, shared resource in the game. Four of the five actions require power, while only the Charge Solar action increases it. Players must therefore plan their energy use carefully.

The Mars Dust Storm Challenge

A special dust storm occurs during Sol 3. During the storm, solar charging becomes less effective. Instead of gaining 18 Power, players gain only 6 Power and use 2 Water.

The storm ends on Sol 4.

This feature teaches players why planning ahead and storing enough energy are important for a Mars mission. It is based on real NASA dust-storm observations, although the game's timing and resource values are simplified for learning purposes.

Winning and Learning from Failure

Players win by keeping all five resources above zero, surviving all five Sols, and successfully returning to Earth.

If any resource reaches zero, the mission fails. The game displays a message explaining the resource problem and helping players understand the consequences of their decisions.

This allows students to learn through experimentation. They can try different strategies, understand what went wrong, and improve their planning.

Tools, Technology, and Development

Our project was developed using:

  • Scratch 3.0: Main programming platform used to develop the game.
  • Scratch coding blocks: Used to program the game rules, resource management, actions, mission stages, and win-or-fail conditions.
  • Vector illustrations: Original artwork created for the project.
  • Synthesized sound effects: Used for the rocket engine, countdown, dust storm, actions, and landings.
  • Web browser: Allows players to access and play the game without installing additional software.

The game includes 21 sound effects and animated rocket journeys to make the experience more interesting and engaging.

Creativity and Unique Features

Our project turns space education into a practical decision-making experience rather than simply presenting information about Mars.

Its creative features include:

  • A complete Earth-to-Mars-to-Earth mission journey.
  • Five astronaut roles linked to five essential resources.
  • Real resource trade-offs for every available action.
  • A special Mars dust storm that changes the best strategy.
  • Live resource information displayed before players make decisions.
  • Animated rocket flights, sound effects, and interactive mission stages.
  • A beginner friendly How to Play screen with six simple rules.
  • A Skip Briefing option for players who want to replay the game.

The combination of resource management, mission storytelling, and interactive learning makes the project engaging for students.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project helps students understand the challenges of living and working on another planet. It develops:

  • Critical thinking: Players must consider the consequences of each decision.
  • Problem-solving: Players find ways to manage limited resources.
  • Planning skills: Players must prepare for future challenges, especially the dust storm.
  • Scientific awareness: Players learn about life-support systems and the challenges of Mars exploration.
  • Decision-making: Players understand that improving one resource can reduce another.

The game is designed for classrooms, science clubs, and families. A complete play session can fit into a classroom activity, making space science more interactive and accessible.

Factors We Considered

While developing the project, we considered the limited availability of resources on Mars, the importance of life-support systems, the need for protection from environmental hazards, and the difficulty of making decisions when resources depend on one another.

We also considered the needs of first-time players. Therefore, we included simple instructions, visible resource costs, clear action labels, animations, and sound effects.

Limitations and Future Improvements

The game is an independent educational project and is not an official NASA product. Its resource values are simplified learning units, not actual NASA mission measurements. Only one NASA dataset is used directly, for the dust-storm observation. The dust storm occurs on a fixed Sol rather than randomly.

Possible future improvements include:

  • Adding a Moon Outpost game mode.
  • Including more NASA datasets and scientific information.
  • Making dust storms and other environmental events more dynamic.
  • Creating a classroom score sheet to compare different survival strategies.

Conclusion

Mars Outpost - The 5-Sol Survival Mission makes learning about space exploration interactive, creative, and challenging. It gives students an opportunity to experience the importance of resource management, teamwork, planning, and problem-solving in a simulated Mars mission.

Our goal is to inspire young learners to think like space explorers and understand that successfully living on another planet requires more than reaching it-it requires keeping the crew safe and bringing everyone home.
